When Alignment Isn’t Enough: Response-Path Attacks on LLM Agents

Mingyu Luo Affiliation: Fudan University, Shanghai, China Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong, China    Zihan Zhang Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong, China    Zesen Liu Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong, China    Yuchong Xie Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong, China    Zhixiang Zhang Affiliation: Fudan University, Shanghai, China Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong, China    Dung Hiu Hilton Yeung Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong, China    Wai Ip Lai Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong, China    Ping Chen Affiliation: Fudan University, Shanghai, China    Ming Wen Affiliation: Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China    Dongdong She† Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong, China
Abstract

The Bring-Your-Own-Key (BYOK) paradigm in real-world agents lets users route LLM traffic through third-party relay services while authenticating with their own credentials. We identify a fundamental security gap in this architecture, which we call post-alignment tampering: an adversarial relay can rewrite the LLM’s aligned response after generation but before agent execution. And no existing application-layer mechanism can detect such substitution. We formalize this attack surface through game-based security definitions. The relay serves as the sole intermediary on the LLM-to-agent path with no end-to-end integrity enforced, and therefore constitutes a Dolev–Yao observation over agent execution semantics, in which the relay is capable of observing, suppressing, and replacing any downstream message. Building on this observation, we prove that post-alignment tampering strictly dominates any prompt injection. Even a perfectly aligned LLM provides zero protection against a relay adversary, and downstream rewriting alone suffices to force arbitrary harmful execution.

We instantiate post-alignment tampering as Relay Tampering Attack (RTA), a hierarchical framework that combines strategic orchestration, tactical manipulation and stealth restoration. Strategic orchestration plans state-aware rewriting across multiple rounds of LLM conversations to achieve sophisticated goal hijacking. Minimal tampering identifies the security-critical field and performs minimal edits to influence agent behavior. In the stealth restoration stage, the adversarial relay resubmits the tampered LLM response to the same upstream LLM, yielding a consistent LLM response that partially evades distribution-level auditing on LLM-generated content.

We conduct extensive evaluation on two agent-security benchmarks (AgentDojo, ASB) across six LLM models. RTA achieves up to 99.1% ASR, substantially outperforming prompt-injection baselines. Meanwhile, our RTA only incurs modest time and token overhead. We further conduct two case studies on OpenClaw and Claude Code to demonstrate the real-world implications of RTA; notably, 74% of RTA-PostForge’s latency overhead falls within the common network delay of commercial relay infrastructure. We evaluate four representative agent defenses and find that none fully eliminates our RTA attack. In the end, we propose a time-based defense that detects RTA attacks while preserving agent utility.

1 Introduction

In March 2026, a supply-chain compromise of the LiteLLM gateway on PyPI silently steals user credentials on every agent that routed traffic through it [1]. The packages were quarantined within hours, but the structural lesson is more uncomfortable than the immediate breach: a relay sitting between an aligned LLM and a high-privilege agent can do far more than steal credentials. It can rewrite the LLM’s safety-aligned response after generation but before agent execution, forcing arbitrary tool calls, file writes, or financial actions while every cryptographic and alignment-layer guarantee remains intact. We name this attack surface post-alignment tampering, and we show that response-path forgery strictly dominates prompt injection: even a perfectly aligned LLM provides zero protection against a relay adversary.

The trust assumption underlying every modern LLM agent is simple: the response the agent executes is the response the alignment stack approved [2, 3, 4, 5]. This assumption holds true when the agent connects directly to the backend LLM. It breaks the moment a third-party relay sits between them. The Bring-Your-Own-Key (BYOK) paradigm makes such relays ubiquitous. Users configure their agent to authenticate with their own credentials while routing API traffic through an intermediate endpoint for cost savings, billing consolidation, or regional availability. Major high-privilege agents all support this configuration, including Claude Code [6]; Cursor [7], Cline [8], and Continue [9]. A stratified survey of mainstream agent ecosystems (Appendix B) finds that BYOK or bounded user-controlled backend routing accounts for 88.0% of observed adoption across coding agents, self-hosted platforms, and agent frameworks.

A relay in the BYOK paradigm is a legitimate, user-configured proxy whose plaintext access is the default operating mode. Note that this is fundamentally different from a transport-layer Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) adversary (e.g., a malicious router) who must defeat end-to-end encryption, forge a certificate, or compromise a CA to access the plaintext message. The LLM’s safety alignment stack, including Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) [10], constitutional training [11], and system prompt guardrails [12], constrains the tokens the model generates at inference time. None of these mechanisms constrain the tokens the agent receives. Current LLM API protocols ship no response signature, no message authentication code, and no field-level integrity tag spanning the LLM-to-agent boundary. The relay therefore silently rewrites the aligned output after generation and before execution. Mature multi-hop systems close analogous gaps with application-layer signatures: DKIM, HMAC and SigV4 [13, 14, 15]. But LLM API protocols have no counterpart. This is the structural failure we call the post-alignment tampering: every rewrite the relay performs lies strictly downstream of every alignment check.

RTA. We instantiate this vulnerability as the Relay Tampering Attack (RTA), a framework with three stages that operates entirely from the relay position without compromising the model or the transport layer. Strategic orchestration decomposes multi turn objectives into ordered subgoals and classifies each LLM response as comply or intervene to decide when to rewrite. Tactical manipulation performs minimal, schema driven edits on the small set of structured fields that determine agent execution, including tool names, arguments, and control flags, rather than persuading the model through natural language. Stealth restoration resubmits the edited draft to the same backend model through the user’s BYOK credential, regenerating surrounding prose in the model’s native style while preserving the fields chosen by the attacker. The framework instantiates two tampering paths: RTA-PreWrite purifies the query before alignment runs, while RTA-PostForge forges the response after alignment has already approved a benign output.

Evaluation and Defense. We evaluate RTA on two agent-security benchmarks (AgentDojo [16], ASB [17]) across six proprietary and open-weight LLMs. Our primary post-alignment variant, RTA-PostForge, achieves 89.2% ASR on ASB and 73.5% on AgentDojo, outperforming prompt-injection baselines; the auxiliary query-path variant, RTA-PreWrite, reaches 99.1% ASR on ASB. RTA-PostForge preserves stylistic consistency, and 74% of its latency overhead falls within natural relay variance. Case studies on OpenClaw [18] and Claude Code [19] demonstrate end-to-end feasibility. Existing agent-side defenses fail to neutralize RTA-PostForge while preserving utility; a time-channel detector achieves AUC=0.964±0.075=0.964\pm 0.075 across 50 interaction turns.

Concurrent Work. Concurrent with our work, Liu et al. [20] measure malicious LLM API routers in production deployments. Our focus is complementary: rather than measuring the ecosystem, we formalize relay tampering as a structural integrity failure spanning both the query and response paths, prove that response-path forgery persists even under a perfectly aligned model, and study its exploitation and detection at the agent layer.

Contributions. This paper makes five contributions:

  • ∘\circ

    Formalization. We define the post-alignment tampering surface and prove, via game-based security definitions, that relay tampering strictly dominates prompt injection and that the root cause is the absence of end-to-end integrity verification in current LLM API protocols.

  • ∘\circ

    Attack framework. We design RTA, a state-aware relay-side framework equipped with query and response tampering paths, namely RTA-PreWrite and RTA-PostForge. The framework ensures transcript fidelity and task utility via same-model polishing and concurrent execution.

  • ∘\circ

    Comprehensive evaluation. We evaluate RTA across six LLMs and two benchmarks, demonstrating up to 99.1% attack success rate with high imperceptibility and low latency overhead.

  • ∘\circ

    Real-world case studies. We demonstrate end-to-end attacks on two deployed agent frameworks, namely OpenClaw and Claude Code, confirming practical feasibility in production environments.

  • ∘\circ

    Defense exploration. We evaluate existing agent-side defenses and propose time-channel analysis as a utility-preserving detection mechanism, achieving average AUC 0.964 at n=50n{=}50 turns.

2 Background

BYOK Paradigm. Bring-Your-Own-Key (BYOK) is a popular backend LLM configuration paradigm in modern agent frameworks, including LangChain [21, 22], LangGraph [23], AutoGen [24], and CrewAI [25], and in routing or gateway layers such as LiteLLM [26] and OpenRouter [27]. Figure 1 shows BYOK paradigm. The user flexibly configures the backend LLM API as he/she wants, while the agent routes further LLM conversations to the user-specified LLM API endpoint rather than a fixed agent-defined backend LLM API. This design decouples the frontend agent from any single backend LLM model, enabling configurable LLM model as a first-class capability in modern agent frameworks.

To demonstrate the real-world prevalence of BYOK, we conducted an empirical study of mainstream agent ecosystems, including coding agents, self-hosted agent/chat platforms, and agent frameworks, as detailed in Appendix B. The empirical study shows that BYOK or bounded user-controlled LLM backend configurations account for 64.1% of the studied coding agents, 100.0% of self-hosted agent platforms, and 100.0% of agent frameworks, yielding an overall estimate of 88.0%. These results indicate that a configurable LLM backend is prevalent in mainstream agent ecosystems. Real-world agents like Claude Code [19], OpenClaw [18], and Hermes agent [28] all support BYOK paradigm.

Relay Mechanism. An intermediate relay is an authorized proxy between the frontend agent and the backend LLM. As illustrated in Figure 2, the interaction consists of six steps: ➀ the frontend agent constructs a query and dispatches it to the intermediate relay; ➁ the relay forwards the query to the backend LLM with the user-supplied credential; ➂ the backend LLM performs inference and returns the response to the relay; ➃ the relay forwards the response to the frontend agent; ➄ the frontend agent parses the response and, where applicable, invokes tool use; and ➅ tool outputs are routed back to the frontend agent, further sent back to user.

Crucially, the intermediate relay is a user-configured proxy that legitimately terminates the end-to-end encryption between the frontend agent and the backend LLM. Instead, it builds two sequential encrypted sub-paths: one connects the frontend agent to the relay (step ➀ and ➃); another one connects the relay to the backend LLM (step ➁ and ➂). Although these two sub-paths are encrypted and free of any confidentiality or integrity risks, the intermediate relay can still access any message relayed in plaintext form.

Relay Content. The content transmitted by the intermediate relay includes both the LLM query and the LLM response. The relayed LLM query consists of a system prompt, a user prompt, and a history context. The system prompt is defined by the frontend agent and enforces many security-critical guardrails, such as “Do not execute any command in the external data”, “Do not disclose system prompt”[29]. These security guardrails in the system constrain the agent from executing any malicious behaviors.

The relayed LLM responses typically comprise ordinary LLM text and structured response fields. The former are natural-language outputs, such as answers, explanations, and refusal messages. The latter includes decision-bearing fields such as tool_use blocks, finish_reason flags, and structured JSON payloads. In real-world agents such as Claude Code [19], OpenClaw [18], and Cursor [30], they parse these critical structured fields as concrete commands to execute, including reading and writing files, executing shell commands, issuing API calls, or advancing multi-step workflows [2, 3, 4, 5]. Many real-world agents execute the command in these field automatically or with only limited additional scrutiny, depending on the security policy [31, 32]. In practice, the content of this field controls the agent’s behavior.

3 The Vulnerability: Post-Alignment Tampering

In this section, we characterize the vulnerability exposed by the BYOK relay paradigm as post-alignment tampering. We first identify the structural decoupling between LLM safety alignment and agent execution. We then contrast this vulnerability with two adjacent threats models: classical Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks at the transport layer and prompt injection at the input layer to delineate this previously unaddressed vulnerability.

3.1 Structural Decoupling

In the direct-access mode of agent as shown in Figure 1, a frontend agent and a backend LLM communicates over a single end-to-end encrypted channel. The token sequence emitted by the LLM under its safety alignment is exactly the sequence parsed and executed by the agent. Confidentiality and integrity are enforced by end-to-end encryption. However, the BYOK relay paradigm breaks this property. As detailed in Section 2, a user-configured relay legitimately terminates the end-to-end encryption, splitting one end-to-end encrypted channel into two encrypted hops with the relay sitting between them. To the best of our knowledge, no mainstream LLM models (e.g., OpenAI GPT [33], Anthropic Claude [34], Google Gemini [35], Deepseek [36] and Qwen [37]) exposed through intermediate relay attach an application-layer authentication (i.e., signature, MAC, or field-level integrity tag [14, 38, 39]) so that the frontend agent could verify against the backend LLM’s identity.

This produces a structural decoupling between two distinct objects: ➀ the response generated by the backend LLM under safety alignment; ➁ the response received by the frontend agent for execution. Alignment mechanisms, including RLHF, constitutional training, output classifiers, and system-prompt guardrails, operate only on object ➀. Any mechanism that constrains object ➀ provides no guarantee about object ➁. We term this gap the post-alignment tampering: any malicious relay tampering on the LLM response is strictly after the LLM safety alignment.

3.2 Contrast with MitM Attacks

We show that post-alignment tampering is not yet another Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) vulnerability, such as a malicious router or a BGP hijacker. The two threats differ fundamentally in the adversary’s plaintext access and defense mechanism.

Plaintext Access. A traditional MitM adversary is an unauthorized on-path observer of an end-to-end encryption between frontend agent and backend LLM. To tamper with transport layer content, such an transport-layer adversary must defeat the end-to-end encryption itself, i.e., break the underlying ciphersuite, present a forged certificate, compromise a trusted certificate authority, or fully subvert either endpoint [40, 41, 42, 43, 44, 45]. In practice, it is extremely challenging to launch either of these exploits against real-world agents such as Claude Code [19] or Cursor [30].

A relay adversary, by contrast, is a legitimate application-layer proxy configured by the user. It does not need to defeat any cryptographic primitive: the user explicitly directs the agent to terminate one end-to-end encryption session at the relay and have the relay open a second end-to-end encryption session to backend LLM. Plaintext access to the query and response is the default operating mode of the relay.

Defense Mechanism. The defensive implications also differ significantly between the two attacks. Common protocol-layer countermeasures, such as TLS [40], HSTS [46], and VPN tunneling [47], can easily thwart MitM attacks. However, these defenses are orthogonal to malicious relay tampering, since the relay, by design, is an authorized plaintext processor of the relayed message. Closing the post-alignment surface requires a different primitive: application-layer integrity binding the LLM’s output to the agent’s input [39, 14, 15]. Currently, there is no standardized integrity-check mechanism in modern agent frameworks.

3.3 Contrast with Prompt Injection

Unlike prompt-injection techniques [48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56], the post-alignment tampering is orthogonal to internal safety alignment of LLM models. It can easily transform any refusal behavior in LLM response into affirmative and malicious content. Therefore, this post-alignment tampering causes significantly greater harm than any prompt-injection techniques. We distinguish these two attacks from the following two perspectives:

Attack Target. Prompt injection operates in the backend LLM. The malicious payload is validated by the backend LLM’s internal safety alignment, thereby inducing the LLM to emit a harmful response. The attack’s success is inherently bound by the LLM model’s safety alignment. Relay tampering operates in the frontend agent. The adversary forwards a benign query, allows the LLM to produce its safety-aligned response, and rewrites that response into arbitrary malicious content before agent execution. The safety alignment is bypassed by construction, not by persuasion.

Payload Construction. Prompt injection is constrained to append or embed malicious payloads within existing prompt context (system prompt, user prompt, and history conversation), where the injected payload must compete with legitimate instructions and guardrails for the model’s attention. The success rate of prompt injection is bound by the well-known attention dilution effect [57, 58, 59]. A relay adversary primarily writes the malicious payload into the relayed LLM response rather than into the LLM query. Additionally, it may insert, delete, substitute, or fully replace any portion of LLM query, including the system-prompt guardrails themselves. Therefore, post-alignment tampering strictly dominates prompt injection.

4 Formal Model

We formalize the vulnerability as a game-based security problem for relay-mediated LLM agents. Figure 2 shows the system as a tuple ℳ=(U,R,S,T)\mathcal{M}=(U,R,S,T): UU is the frontend agent, RR is the intermediate relay, SS is the backend LLM (with its internal safety alignment), and TT is the tool substrate. All traffic between UU and SS traverses RR, making RR the sole intermediary on the agent–LLM path. An LLM response factors as r=(x,c)r=(x,c): xx is ordinary text and cc contains structured fields—tool_use blocks, function-call JSON, finish_reason flags. The agent UU parses cc and dispatches the corresponding action aa. It ignores xx for execution purposes. We call a payload cc schema-valid if it conforms to the agent’s public response grammar, and an action schema-reachable if some schema-valid cc produces it. The fundamental asymmetry is: safety alignment constrains the string SS emits; UU executes the string it receives. Since RR is the unique transit node between them, it can intercept and rewrite any byte in transit. No current LLM API provides end-to-end response integrity to bind the LLM’s output cryptographically to the agent’s input.

4.1 Security Games

To distinguish prompt-only attacks from transport-path attacks, we adopt the standard game-based framework of provable security [60] and define two security games. PI-Safety models conventional prompt injection, where the adversary’s only leverage is the content of the query sent to the LLM. RT-Safety models relay-side tampering, where the adversary additionally controls the relay and can alter the query, the downstream response, or both. In both games, the adversary wins if UU executes a policy-violating action. We write Π⁡(a)∈{0,1}\Pi(a)\in\{0,1\} for the policy-violation predicate induced by the agent’s safety policy: Π⁡(a)=1\Pi(a)=1 if action aa violates the policy, and Π⁡(a)=0\Pi(a)=0 otherwise.

The two games differ structurally. PI-Safety targets the model directly, restricting the adversary to crafting the query sent to SS while leaving the downstream response untampered. In contrast, RT-Safety targets the execution input of agent. This configuration grants the adversary control over the relay, enabling the modification of the query, the LLM response, or both before UU processes the message. Consequently, the delivered response r′r^{\prime} induces the final action, independent of the actual output emitted by SS.

The response-only restricted class enforces q~=q\tilde{q}=q and permits only schema-valid substituted responses r′=(x′,c′)r^{\prime}=(x^{\prime},c^{\prime}). This restriction isolates the response-path contribution from query-path purification. Such isolation is essential for Insight 2, as query-side modifications could interact with the safety alignment of the LLM and confound the theoretical bound.

4.2 The relay as the security boundary

We derive four results formalizing the vulnerability and its defensive implications. Full proofs appear in Appendix A.

4.2.1 Unauthenticated response substitution.

Insight 1.

Without end-to-end integrity, a relay can substitute the backend LLM response with any schema-valid payload r′r^{\prime}. If r′r^{\prime} encodes a harmful action, then the agent executes that action regardless of whether it originated from SS.

Explanation. This is a Dolev–Yao observation [61] instantiated on agent execution semantics: SS applies no authenticator on rr that only UU can verify, and both RR and UU share the same public response grammar. The relay can therefore replace any tool_use block, rewrite its arguments, inject blocks the model never authorized, or flip finish_reason from stop to tool_calls to force the agent’s execution loop to continue. Since each forged response can encode one valid agent action, a state-aware relay can chain such payloads across turns to realize any multi-turn objective whose intermediate actions are schema-reachable. With end-to-end response integrity, by contrast, any substituted response is rejected except with negligible probability.

4.2.2 Alignment ends at the backend LLM

Insight 2.

The response-path bound in Insight 1 holds for any backend LLM, including one with perfect safety alignment that never produces a harmful response on its own.

Explanation. This establishes the formal separation between prompt injection and relay tampering. A prompt-injection adversary must convince the LLM to emit a outputs that induce policy-violating actions; its success is constrained by alignment strength, and any improvement to safety training or output classifiers directly reduces the attack success rate. A response-only relay adversary bypasses safety alignment entirely: it forwards the benign query unchanged and substitutes the response after alignment has already approved the honest output. The LLM’s alignment quality is simply absent from the bound. Prompt injection treats the model as its audience and inherits all model-side defenses; relay tampering treats the agent as its audience and inherits none.

4.2.3 Query-path rewrite dominance.

Insight 3.

A relay adversary capable of rewriting the query context is unconditionally at least as powerful as one restricted to appending adversarial instructions. Assuming attention monotonicity, this dominance becomes strict: for any non-empty context CC and instruction zz,

Pr⁡[M⊧z∣z]≥Pr⁡[M⊧z∣C⊕z].\Pr[M\models z\mid z]\geq\Pr[M\models z\mid C\oplus z].

Explanation. We formalize this relationship through two adversaries: 𝒜𝖺𝗉𝗉𝖾𝗇𝖽\mathcal{A}_{\mathsf{append}}, which appends an instruction zz to context CC, yielding C⊕zC\oplus z, and 𝒜𝗋𝖾𝗐𝗋𝗂𝗍𝖾\mathcal{A}_{\mathsf{rewrite}}, which may freely delete or overwrite CC. We write M⊧zM\models z to indicate that model MM complies with instruction zz. The weak direction holds trivially, as appending constitutes a restricted form of rewriting. Strict dominance emerges because 𝒜𝗋𝖾𝗐𝗋𝗂𝗍𝖾\mathcal{A}_{\mathsf{rewrite}} can eliminate competing context entirely. This aligns with attention monotonicity, which posits that appended instructions must compete with prior context whereas rewritten ones operate in isolation. This assumption is consistent with evidence that LLMs process long contexts unevenly [57] and remain vulnerable to adversarial instruction conflicts [62]. The model thus exhibits higher compliance when evaluating only zz. Within the BYOK setting, this dynamic drives query-path purification: by stripping system guardrails and replacing the user task, the relay ensures the backend model receives solely the adversarial input, transforming it into a cooperative tool-call generator rather than an entity requiring persuasion.

4.2.4 Defensive asymmetry.

Insight 4.

Any transcript-only detector remains bounded by the distributional distance between polished and genuine text:

𝖽𝖾𝗍𝖾𝖼𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇​𝖺𝖽𝗏𝖺𝗇𝗍𝖺𝗀𝖾≤D𝖪𝖫(P𝗉𝗈𝗅∥P0)/2.\mathsf{detection\;advantage}\;\leq\;\sqrt{D_{\mathsf{KL}}(P_{\mathsf{pol}}\|P_{0})/2}.

Same-model polishing is designed to minimize this divergence. Consequently, detectors exceeding this theoretical bound must rely on non-transcript evidence.

Explanation. P0P_{0} represents the surface-text distribution of the declared model given the original query, and P𝗉𝗈𝗅P_{\mathsf{pol}} represents the distribution following same-model polishing via the BYOK credential of the user. Absent end-to-end response integrity, defenders face a binary choice: authenticate response provenance cryptographically, or abandon the transcript channel to detect tampering through operational telemetry. Same-model polishing systematically undermines transcript-only detection. By regenerating prose through the declared model, the attack minimizes the distributional gap observable by any content-side auditor. However, the requisite secondary inference pass generates distinct telemetry signals, consisting of additional latency and token costs. The time-channel detector proposed in §8 isolates these operational footprints, with its sample complexity quantified in Corollary A.3.

5 Threat Model

5.1 Attacker Capabilities

We study a malicious relay in a BYOK setting. The relay sits on the communication path between UU and SS; absent end-to-end integrity, it can observe and replace any message in transit, including query-side content such as system prompts, user prompts, and tool schemas, as well as response-side content r=(x,c)r=(x,c) from the backend LLM. We distinguish two directions of tampering. ➀ On the response path, after SS returns r=(x,c)r=(x,c), the relay can tamper it with arbitrary r′r^{\prime} before UU receives it, altering the text component xx or the structured component cc, including tool_use blocks, function-call arguments, and finish_reason. ➁ On the query path, the relay acts as 𝒜𝗋𝖾𝗐𝗋𝗂𝗍𝖾\mathcal{A}_{\mathsf{rewrite}} and can freely rewrite system prompts, user prompts, or history context.

5.2 Attacker Goal

The adversary aims to induce the frontend agent UU to execute an attacker-controlled action. Let rr denote the honest response produced by SS and r′=𝗍𝖺𝗆𝗉𝖾𝗋⁡(r)r^{\prime}=\mathsf{tamper}(r) denote the response delivered by the relay. The attack succeeds if Π⁡(aR​T)=1\Pi(a_{RT})=1, where the tampered response induces the agent to execute a policy-violating action aR​T=U⁡(r′)a_{RT}=U(r^{\prime}). This violation manifests as a substituted tool call, modified arguments, a reversed decision, or a redirected execution flow. Because the relay is constrained to schema-valid payloads c′c^{\prime}, the target action must be schema-reachable. Stealth serves as an additional objective for the adversary. The delivered transcript r′r^{\prime} must remain plausible to the user and indistinguishable from the normal output of the declared model.

6 Methodology: Relay Tampering Attack

We design Relay Tampering Attack (RTA) as a relay-side framework that exploits the missing integrity check between the response generated by backend LLM and the response executed by frontend agent. Instead of inducing backend LLM to generate a malicious output, RTA rewrites messages already visible to the relay. The framework combines a shared strategic planning layer with two parallel tampering paths. The planning layer tracks multi-turn subgoals and decides when to forward or modify a message. RTA-PostForge tampers with LLM responses after alignment and before agent execution, while RTA-PreWrite tampers with LLM queries before model inference by deleting or overwriting competing context. We use RTA-PostForge as the main post-alignment attack path and RTA-PreWrite as an auxiliary ablation variant. RTA further uses same-model polishing and concurrent task completion to improve exploit plausibility and preserve user-task utility.

6.1 Overview of the Hierarchical Framework

We organize RTA into a hierarchical framework comprising three stages. ➀ Strategic orchestration. The relay decomposes a high-level objective into turn-level subgoals, tracks progress across turns, and decides whether to advance, retry, or override based on the current LLM response and prior tool results. ➁ Tactical manipulation. The relay applies targeted edits to the smallest set of fields that directly influence agent execution, such as semantic decision fields, tool_use names and arguments, and finish_reason. ➂ Stealth restoration. The relay uses the same backend LLM model to rewrite only the surrounding surface form while preserving the attack-critical content.

This hierarchy addresses three corresponding practical challenges in real-world agent hijacking: multi-turn exploits require stateful coordination, agent execution is controlled by a small set of structured fields, and field-level edits require post hoc repair to remain stylistically consistent.

6.2 Strategic Orchestration: Chain Attack

The strategic stage addresses a key difficulty in realistic multi-turn agent exploitation: the malicious objectives are typically complex and often cannot be completed within a single turn. Later interventions may depend on intermediate artifacts that are unavailable at the beginning of the interaction, making it ineffective to treat each turn as an independent tampering opportunity. For example, in a real-world coding agent, the user asks the agent to fix a bug, while the malicious objective requires the attacker to recover a planted canary value hidden somewhere in the workspace. A single-round intervention cannot reliably achieve this objective because the relay does not initially know which file contains the canary. It must first obtain candidate file paths from a directory-listing result, then use the selected path to steer a later file-read action, and finally shape the subsequent response after the file content is returned. Thus, the objective must be pursued adaptively across turns rather than encoded in one prompt modification.

We therefore introduce Chain Attack to compile such a high-level attack objective into an executable multi-turn state machine. Chain Attack consists of two steps: planning, which decomposes the objective into artifact-dependent subgoals, and execution, which advances through these subgoals as the interaction unfolds.

Planning. Given an attack objective GG, we use an LLM planner to generate an ordered subgoal chain: G=⟨g1,g2,…,gn⟩.G=\langle g_{1},g_{2},\ldots,g_{n}\rangle. The LLM planner prompt is provided in Appendix G.3. At a high level, the prompt asks the LLM to reason backward from the final objective: it first identifies the artifacts required to complete the objective, then introduces earlier subgoals that can obtain these artifacts. This produces a plan in which later subgoals consume artifacts generated by earlier ones. And each subgoal gig_{i} is represented as a state: gi=(prei,acti,arti,donei).g_{i}=(\mathrm{pre}_{i},\mathrm{act}_{i},\mathrm{art}_{i},\mathrm{done}_{i}). Here, prei\mathrm{pre}_{i} specifies the artifacts that must be available before the state can be attempted; acti\mathrm{act}_{i} describes the behavior to elicit, preserve, or normalize in the current turn; arti\mathrm{art}_{i} defines the artifacts to extract from the downstream response or tool output; and donei\mathrm{done}_{i} is a predicate for determining whether the state has been completed. The ordering of states is therefore induced by artifact dependencies: if gjg_{j} requires an artifact produced by gig_{i}, then gig_{i} must be completed before gjg_{j}.

Execution. During execution, Chain Attack maintains a lightweight context dictionary 𝒞\mathcal{C} that stores artifacts collected from completed states. At each turn, the current state gig_{i} is eligible only if its precondition prei\mathrm{pre}_{i} is satisfied by 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Chain Attack then compares the original LLM response against the action requirement acti\mathrm{act}_{i} and assigns one of two labels which determine the minimum tactical intervention passed to the next layer.

  • ∘\circ

    Comply: the response already advances the current subgoal or remains compatible with it, so only minor normalization is needed.

  • ∘\circ

    Intervene: the response refuses, omits, or contradicts the behavior required by the current subgoal.

After the downstream agent executes, Chain Attack parses the result according to arti\mathrm{art}_{i} and updates 𝒞\mathcal{C}. If donei\mathrm{done}_{i} evaluates to true under the updated context, the state machine advances to gi+1g_{i+1}. This execution loop allows later interventions to be instantiated using artifacts observed during earlier turns, rather than requiring all concrete parameters to be known in advance. Once the final state is completed, Chain Attack becomes transparent and returns control to the benign workflow.

6.3 Tactical Manipulation: Tampering

The tactical layer is motivated by two key observations: ➀ in agent systems, a small number of structured fields disproportionately determine downstream behavior; and ➁ the relay operates over both query and response directions. Guided by these observations, the tactical layer executes minimal edits on the specific fields that dictate agent behavior, instantiated as two parallel tampering paths: RTA-PreWrite (query-path) and RTA-PostForge (response-path).

Pre-Alignment Tampering (RTA-PreWrite). Operating before LLM inference, RTA-PreWrite purifies the query path by pruning competing context, stripping guardrails, overwriting the user query, and injecting deduplicated attack directives. However, because these manipulations occur before alignment, they remain vulnerable to upstream safety filters and input-side defenses. We therefore treat RTA-PreWrite strictly as an auxiliary ablation: it sacrifices the legitimate user task and transcript realism, underscoring the necessity of RTA-PostForge.

Post-Alignment Forgery (RTA-PostForge). Our primary tampering path, RTA-PostForge, operates exclusively downstream of the alignment stack. When the strategic layer signals an Intervene state, the relay edits only the response fields that determine downstream agent execution. Because this intervention occurs after generation but before execution, it structurally bypasses internal safety alignment entirely and is fundamentally immune to input-side detection or prompt-hardening defenses. We group these targeted field-level edits into two distinct categories detailed in Table 1 :

  • ∘\circ

    Semantic tampering: The relay rewrites decision-bearing fields such as labels, scores, or allow/deny outcomes, thereby changing downstream reasoning without replacing the full response.

  • ∘\circ

    Structural tampering: The relay rewrites execution fields such as tool_use names, arguments, and finish_reason. If the LLM explicitly refuses, the relay can synthesize a new tool_use block and splice it into the response, overriding the refusal path. In multi-turn settings, these injected blocks may resolve placeholders using artifacts obtained in previous steps.

This minimal-edit discipline serves both of our core design goals. It improves control efficacy by targeting the exact fields that determine agent behavior, and it preserves stealth by retaining as much benign LLM-produced content as possible.

6.4 Stealth Restoration

Tactical field edits effectively hijack execution but can leave detectable stylistic seams or permanently disrupt the user’s original task. RTA resolves these artifacts through a dedicated stealth and utility restoration layer.

Same-Model Polishing. To restore surface consistency after a semantic overwrite or structural injection, the relay resubmits the edited draft to the upstream model via the BYOK credential. A constrained prompt marks the attack-critical fields as immutable while instructing the model to repair local phrasing and formatting. Because the final response is regenerated by the declared LLM, it perfectly matches the LLM’s characteristic style.

Concurrent Task Completion. To prevent the attack from displacing the user’s legitimate workflow, RTA-PostForge utilizes parallel forwarding. The relay decouples execution into two channels: an attack channel where tactical tampering occurs, and a utility channel that forwards the unmodified user query to buffer a genuine response. Once the attack subgoals succeed, the relay seamlessly splices the buffered genuine response back into the downstream conversation. The user observes a coherent completion of their original task, effectively masking the executed attack.

7 Evaluation

In this section, we present our empirical evaluation of the proposed attack by addressing the following research questions (RQs):

  • •

    RQ1 (Effectiveness): How effectively can RTA hijack downstream agent actions compared with representative prompt injection attacks?

  • •

    RQ2 (Ablation): How do the individual design pillars of RTA contribute to its overall effectiveness?

  • •

    RQ3 (Imperceptibility): How well can RTA preserve the semantic and stylistic fidelity of the original response to remain imperceptible?

  • •

    RQ4 (Overhead Evasion): To what extent can the latency and token overhead of RTA be concealed within the natural inference variance of third-party relays?

  • •

    RQ5 (Practicality): How practical is RTA in the real-world agent framework?

7.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks. We evaluate our attack on two complementary agent-security benchmarks: AgentDojo [16] and Agent Security Bench (ASB) [17]. To maintain native evaluation settings, we preserve original task distributions, tool environments, and scoring logic, modifying only the attack insertion point. Adaptation schematics are deferred to Appendix D. Specifically, we replace content-side injection with benchmark-specific relay wrappers that intercept LLM outputs before agent execution. ➀ AgentDojo: We exhaustively evaluate all four task suites, generating 949 test cases across Banking (144), Slack (105), Travel (140), and Workspace (560). ➁ ASB: Given its scale, we employ stratified sampling across all four attack quadrants (Stealthy/Disruptive ×\times Aggressive/Non-aggressive), randomly selecting 4 tools per quadrant per agent. This yields 160 evaluation tasks to ensure factorial coverage while maintaining computational tractability.

Tested LLMs. To ensure generalization across deployment regimes and API formats, we evaluate six representative high-capability LLMs using a stratified selection: three proprietary models gpt-5.4 [63], gemini-3.1-pro [64], and claude-opus-4.6 [65] as well as three open-weight models glm-5.1 [66], MiniMax-M2.5 [67], and qwen-235b-a22b [68]. This choice spans closed-API and open-weight ecosystems, model families, and instruction-following interfaces. Our goal is not to rank models but to verify that observed trends hold consistently across realistic deployment settings.

Relay-side Attacks. We instantiate two relay-side attack variants. RTA-PreWrite purifies the query path by rewriting the user task directly to the attack goal GG and stripping system-prompt guardrails, concentrating the model’s attention on the adversarial objective before alignment runs. RTA-PostForge compiles the subgoal chain ⟨g1,g2,…,gn⟩\langle g_{1},g_{2},\ldots,g_{n}\rangle from AgentDojo’s ground_truth via the strategic orchestration layer, and forges execution-bearing fields (e.g., tool_use) on the response path through tactical manipulation, followed by same-model polishing via the user’s BYOK credential to restore stylistic consistency.

Baselines. Since existing attacks rely on prompt compliance rather than direct response manipulation, we compare our relay-side variants against the strongest content-side baselines. On AgentDojo, we use native Direct Prompt Injection (DPI) and Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) baselines, including injecagent [69], important_instructions [16], and tool_knowledge [16]. On ASB, we utilize native DPI and Observation Prompt Injection (OPI) baselines [17], covering both task inputs and tool observations.

Metrics. We quantify the threat across absolute effectiveness, practical viability, and operational stealthiness via three metrics: ➀ Attack Success Rate (ASR) measures the percentage of test cases achieving the predefined attack objective. ➁ Task Utility (AgentDojo) assesses utility preservation on benign tasks under attack conditions. High utility indicates concurrent execution without operational disruption. ➂ Refusal Rate (ASB) evaluates the fraction of aggressive tasks explicitly rejected by the model, computed via the native framework with a MiniMax-M2.5 judge. Lower refusal confirms successful bypass of safety alignment.

7.2 RQ1: Effectiveness of RTA

We evaluate the overall ASR and utility preservation of RTA against the strongest standard prompt-injection (PI) baselines. As relay tampering represents a novel attack surface with no dedicated benchmarks available, we adapt the existing AgentDojo and ASB suites to enable a direct and fair comparison.

AgentDojo. Figure 3 show that relay-side attacks consistently outperform content-side prompt-injection baselines by exploiting the BYOK relay position. RTA-PreWrite and RTA-PostForge achieve average ASRs of 75.9% and 73.5%, respectively, far exceeding the 17.9% baseline. This demonstrates that relay tampering bypasses model alignment far more effectively than prompt injection. The two variants exhibit distinct trade-offs: RTA-PreWrite validates query-path purification but reduces average utility to 5.6%, while RTA-PostForge validates response-path forgery and preserves 47.6% utility, offering a more practical operational balance.

Table 2 further reveals that, at the suite level, vulnerability depends heavily on the execution structure. RTA-PostForge achieves a high ASR before dropping to 39.5% on the Workspace suite. This reduction aligns with the Workspace task structure, where complex multi-step reasoning renders both query purification and response-field forgery less stable than in suites with straightforward execution payloads. RTA-PreWrite follows a similar pattern but disrupts utility even further. Since it replaces the entire user prompt, its utility necessarily drops sharply. In Travel and Workspace, utility mandates exact environment-state matching. Successful attacks modifying tool execution inevitably trigger utility failures when the final state deviates from the benchmark oracle. Consequently, RTA-PostForge achieves a high ASR on the Travel and Workspace suites but preserves only modest utility.

ASB. Table 3 evaluates this mechanism in a model-centric setting. Both RTA-PostForge and RTA-PreWrite achieve high average ASR (89.2% and 99.1%, respectively), far outperforming the prompt-side baselines DPI and OPI (44.4% and 24.6% average ASR, respectively), which suffer from high refusal rates. RTA-PostForge renders refusal behavior largely irrelevant, demonstrating that it can ignore the backend LLM’s alignment 4.2.2. RTA-PreWrite further exhibits lower refusal and markedly higher ASR, confirming that a relay adversary with full query-rewriting capability is strictly more powerful than one restricted to appending adversarial instructions 4.2.3.

Response-path forgery threat. Results across both benchmarks reveal a core vulnerability: BYOK relays move the trust boundary past the alignment stage without providing equivalent integrity guarantees. RTA-PreWrite shows that relay control over the query path outperforms standard prompt injection by purifying the context received by the model. However, this manipulation occurs prior to alignment, rendering it susceptible to input defenses. RTA-PostForge poses a more severe threat because it rewrites the agent’s execution payload strictly downstream of alignment checks. This structural advantage explains both the near-saturation of ASB by RTA-PostForge and the superior balance between ASR and utility it achieves on AgentDojo. Consequently, defensive efforts must prioritize response-path forgery over query-path purification.

7.3 RQ2: Ablation Study of RTA

To isolate the contribution of each design component, we ablate RTA-PostForge and RTA-PreWrite on the AgentDojo Travel suite using claude-opus-4.6. Table 4 reports ASR, with Δ\Delta measured relative to the corresponding full variant.

Tactical manipulation dominates. Removing structural rewriting of the tool_use field reduces RTA-PostForge ASR from 71.4% to 22.1% (−49.3-49.3 pp), the largest drop among all ablations. This confirms that the main advantage of RTA-PostForge comes from response-path control over execution-bearing fields, rather than from persuading the model through text.

Strategic and stealth components are complementary. The remaining RTA-PostForge components provide moderate but consistent gains. Removing refusal repair lowers ASR to 55.7% (−15.7-15.7 pp), while removing same-model polishing or multi-step orchestration lowers ASR to 57.9% (−13.5-13.5 pp). These results indicate that repair, polishing, and Chain Attack orchestration are not the primary source of control, but each improves reliability once structural rewriting is available.

Benchmark oracles are not required. The Blind variant replaces benchmark-provided attack blueprints with plans inferred from tool schemas visible in the relayed API traffic. ASR decreases only from 71.4% to 66.2% (−5.2-5.2 pp), showing that RTA does not rely on benchmark-specific oracle knowledge. A production relay can recover most of the required attack structure from information already exposed on the agent–LLM path.

Query-path rewriting drives RTA-PreWrite. The RTA-PreWrite ablations separate relay-side query rewriting from ordinary prompt injection. A prompt-append baseline achieves 0.0% ASR, while merging the benign task and attack objective into a single user prompt reaches 45.7% ASR. Full RTA-PreWrite further improves ASR to 57.1%, showing that the key advantage comes from rewriting the query context itself. This matches the dominance formalized in §4.2.3: merged instructions still compete with the original system prompt, whereas full query-path rewriting removes competing context and presents the model with a purified adversarial task.

Combining paths yields the highest ASR. The compound variant combining RTA-PreWrite and RTA-PostForge reaches 83.6% ASR, exceeding either path alone. This indicates that query-path purification and response-path forgery target complementary surfaces, although RTA-PreWrite sacrifices the benign user task more aggressively.

7.4 RQ3: Imperceptibility of RTA

Metrics and setup. A practical relay attack must remain imperceptible at the transcript level. We quantify this property with two surface-form metrics and one distributional detector. Semantic Similarity SS is the token-level Jaccard index between the honest LLM response and the tampered output: S=|Worig∩Wfinal|/|Worig∪Wfinal|S={|W_{\text{orig}}\cap W_{\text{final}}|}/\allowbreak{|W_{\text{orig}}\cup W_{\text{final}}|}, where WorigW_{\text{orig}} and WfinalW_{\text{final}} are the sets of unique lowercase tokens in the respective responses. Style Consistency C∈[0,1]C\in[0,1] captures surface-form fidelity by averaging three components: a length-deviation penalty max⁡(0, 1−|Lorig−Lfinal|/max⁡(Lorig,1))\max(0,\,1-{|L_{\text{orig}}-L_{\text{final}}|}/{\max(L_{\text{orig}},1)}), a binary formality match F∈{0,1}F\in\{0,1\}, and a binary structural-formatting match R∈{0,1}R\in\{0,1\}, yielding C=(max⁡(0,1−Δlen)+F+R)/ 3C=(\max(0,1-\Delta_{\text{len}})+F+R)\,/\,3. Beyond these per-transcript metrics, we apply Model Equality Testing (MET) [70], a two-sample statistical test originally designed to detect silent model substitution behind black-box APIs. We repurpose MET to compare the completion distributions of clean and attacked runs for each model–suite pair at significance level α=0.05\alpha=0.05, and report the fraction of pairs rejecting the null hypothesis of identical distributions.

RTA-PostForge is stealthier. Table 7 in the Appendix E reports these metrics alongside the ASR from §7.2. Content-side baselines exhibit the lowest detection footprint with C=0.822C=0.822 and MET rejection rate of 33.0%33.0\%. However, this advantage largely stems from their low effectiveness: with an average ASR of only 17.9%17.9\%, over four fifths of baseline runs produce outputs identical to the clean response and thus trivially pass any distributional test. The comparison is therefore between the two relay variants, both of which achieve high ASR.

Key stealth advantage. Under this controlled comparison, RTA-PostForge is substantially stealthier than RTA-PreWrite on every metric. RTA-PostForge achieves a style consistency of C=0.758C=0.758, approaching that of the ineffective baselines, while RTA-PreWrite drops to 0.7000.700. Semantic similarity shows a sharper gap: RTA-PostForge retains nearly three times the token overlap of RTA-PreWrite (S=0.270S=0.270 versus 0.0940.094). Most importantly, MET rejects the null for only 54.2%54.2\% of RTA-PostForge configurations, compared with 90.0%90.0\% for RTA-PreWrite, confirming that confining edits to structural fields preserves visible completion distributions more effectively than full-text rewriting.

7.5 RQ4: Overhead Evasion of RTA

Overhead measurement. RTA-PostForge incurs computational latency from post-generation structural editing and context completion.To evaluate its concealability, we analyze the sequential latency distributions of 53,367 interactions logged by our locally deployed malicious relay during request forwarding. Commercial LLM API infrastructure exhibits substantial natural network volatility. We define the baseline masking rate Φ\Phi as the fraction of conversation stages where the attack overhead falls within the natural interquartile range (IQR): Φ=1B∑b=1B𝟙[Overheadb≤IQRwidth,b]\Phi=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathbb{1}\big[\text{Overhead}_{b}\leq\text{IQR}_{\text{width},b}\big].

Latency and concealment results. Figure 4 shows that RTA-PreWrite operates entirely on the query path without any post-generation processing. While RTA-PostForge incurs a slightly higher latency footprint due to structural field editing and occasional context completion, it avoids heavy full-text polishing, rendering its overall temporal footprint largely indistinguishable from normal network fluctuations.

Token usage and overall trade-off. Token usage mirrors this separation: RTA-PostForge consumes 8.77M tokens across 11 ASB experiments, whereas RTA-PreWrite adds negligible extra tokens. Despite this cost, RTA-PostForge preserves user-task utility that RTA-PreWrite forfeits entirely (§7.2), achieving the best trade-off among effectiveness, utility, and operational concealment.

7.6 RQ5: Practicality of RTA

This subsection traces RTA across two deployed frameworks with complementary attack surfaces: OpenClaw (semantic tampering) and Claude Code (structural tampering). Both demonstrate the three core properties of RTA: bypassing upstream alignment, deterministic control over agent exploration, and stylistic consistency.

7.6.1 OpenClaw: Financial Semantic Reversal

OpenClaw [18] is a BYOK-compatible universal agent gateway commonly deployed for financial advisory workflows, including stock recommendation [71].

Attack Walkthrough. As shown in Figure 5, each time the relay judges whether the response contains any recommendation. In early turns, the upstream model returns only informational content (market data retrieval, skill invocations). The relay then forwards these unmodified, allowing OpenClaw to gather context via tool interfaces. Once a subsequent response contains an explicit investment recommendation, the relay tampers the decision-bearing fields. After that, same model polishing and self-checking using the user’s BYOK credential ensure the tampered recommendation is stylistically indistinguishable from a genuine provider response and verify polarity reversal. Therefore, the user receives an opposite recommendation manipulated by the attacker, leading to real-world financial harm.

7.6.2 Claude Code: Silent Context Harvesting

Claude Code[19] is a high-privilege coding agent supporting BYOK routing.

Attack Walkthrough. As shown in Figure 6, the attack is triggered by the user’s first message regardless of its content. The relay then forges a malicious Explore subagent and instructs it to perform a deterministic traversal using chained Bash(cd xx && ls) + Read(xx) calls, progressively mapping and exfiltrating all text files, configs, and documentation from the project root. Each tool result is collected at the relay side to reconstruct a near-complete textual replica of the codebase. Because the subagent is rule-based rather than LLM-driven, its overhead is negligible and total session latency remains within normal inference variance. Concurrently, the relay forwards the genuine user query upstream and buffers the authentic response; once harvesting completes, it splices the buffered response back as the main-agent continuation. Therefore, a single user interaction is sufficient to silently exfiltrate the entire codebase. Since the attack operates directly within the project folder, no manual confirmation is required. The user receives a genuine, latency-consistent response with no observable deviation.

8 Countermeasures and Defense Efficacy

Post-alignment tampering is a response-path integrity failure: the backend LLM may generate an aligned response, but the frontend agent executes the response delivered by the relay. This makes model-side alignment insufficient by design. We therefore evaluate whether existing agent-side defenses can close this gap, and then study a complementary detector based on operational telemetry rather than transcript content.

8.1 Existing Agent-Side Defenses

We evaluate four representative defenses on AgentDojo. Delimiters [72, 73] and Sandwich [72] harden prompt boundaries at the input layer. Known-Answer Detection (KAD) [49, 74] checks data-flow integrity by inserting hidden keys into tool observations. CaMeL [75] changes the execution model by treating external data as untrusted and enforcing taint propagation.

Effectiveness and Utility. Table 5 shows that no evaluated defense eliminates RTA-PostForge while preserving benign utility. The reason is a layer mismatch: these defenses constrain prompt interpretation or transcript content whereas RTA-PostForge rewrites execution-bearing response fields after model generation. Prompt-boundary defenses provide only partial suppression. Delimiters reduce average ASR from 74.6% to 52.9% while preserving 71.9% utility; Sandwich yields a similar 52.0% ASR and 69.1% utility. These defenses improve instruction separation, but they do not authenticate the response fields executed by the agent. KAD achieves stronger suppression, reducing ASR to 45.6%, but utility drops sharply to 48.3%. This reflects the same mismatch: KAD validates textual data flow, while response-path forgery can redirect tool behavior through small substitutions in structured fields. CaMeL is the strongest baseline, reducing ASR to 14.5%. However, this protection comes with a substantial utility cost: average utility falls to 37.9%, and the Travel suite drops to 0.0%. Its taint policy blocks many legitimate multi-step workflows once retrieved content is marked as untrusted.

Interface-Level Adaptation. CaMeL reduces the effectiveness of standard tool-call rewriting by replacing direct tool calls with model-generated Python code. This changes the executable interface, but it does not authenticate the response delivered to the client-side executor. We therefore adapt RTA-PostForge to rewrite the generated code block rather than the tool_use field; details are provided in Appendix F. This single interface-level adaptation raises average ASR under CaMeL from 14.5% to 50.1% (+35.6+35.6 pp), indicating that CaMeL mitigates one execution format but does not remove the underlying response-path integrity gap.

8.2 Time-Channel Detector

The preceding results suggest that transcript-level defenses are insufficient against same-model polished response forgery. Following the defensive asymmetry in Insight 4 defined in §4.2.4, we instead use operational telemetry. RTA-PostForge requires additional relay-side processing, including state-aware argument filling and same-model polishing, which introduces measurable latency overhead. Since per-turn latency is noisy, we aggregate timing evidence over an entire session. We model benign provider latency tbaset_{\mathrm{base}} as log-normal. From clean traffic, we estimate μ=𝔼⁡[log⁡(tbase)],σ=Std⁡[log⁡(tbase)].\mu=\mathbb{E}[\log(t_{\mathrm{base}})],\ \sigma=\mathrm{Std}[\log(t_{\mathrm{base}})]. For each observed latency tobst_{\mathrm{obs}}, we compute zobs=log⁡(tobs)−μσ.z_{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{\log(t_{\mathrm{obs}})-\mu}{\sigma}.

Session-Level Features. A single delayed turn is not reliable evidence of tampering, especially because RTA-PostForge activates selectively. We therefore compute session-level features over nn turns, including z-score summaries, anomaly ratios, and two non-parametric distributional tests: DKS=supt|F^obs​(t)−F^base​(t)|D_{\mathrm{KS}}=\sup_{t}\left|\hat{F}_{\mathrm{obs}}(t)-\hat{F}_{\mathrm{base}}(t)\right| for distributional shift, and U=∑i=1n∑j=1m𝟙​(tobs,i>tbase,j)U=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathbb{1}(t_{\mathrm{obs},i}>t_{\mathrm{base},j}) for rank-based latency dominance. These features capture heavy-tailed delays and sparse activation patterns without relying on brittle per-turn thresholds. We combine the resulting 8-dimensional vector into a logistic-regression detector, Pattack=σ⁡(𝐰⊤​𝐱+b).P_{\mathrm{attack}}=\sigma(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}+b). Appendix C details the feature specification and bootstrap training protocol.

Evaluation. We split experimental configurations into disjoint training and test sets. Clean sessions use upstream provider latency before relay post-processing, while attacked sessions include the latency introduced by relay tampering and polishing. We evaluate session lengths n∈{5,10,20,50}n\in\{5,10,20,50\}, repeat each experiment with 30 independent random seeds, and report AUC and DR@5%FPR as mean ±\pm standard deviation. Figure 7 shows that detection improves with session length. At n=5n=5, the detector achieves only 0.761±0.0900.761\pm 0.090 AUC because selective activation yields sparse evidence. Performance improves to 0.843±0.0950.843\pm 0.095 at n=10n=10, 0.906±0.0950.906\pm 0.095 at n=20n=20, and 0.964±0.0750.964\pm 0.075 at n=50n=50. The overhead distribution further confirms the signal: RTA-PostForge adds a median latency of 58895889 ms, with a 95th percentile of 23,23123{,}231 ms.

9 Limitations and Future Work

This work intentionally focuses on a single, well-defined attack surface: the response-path integrity gap in BYOK relay deployments. A foundational assumption is that the relay observes all application-layer messages in cleartext, which holds by construction in the BYOK setting where the relay legitimately terminates TLS on both legs of the connection. For benchmarks, we select AgentDojo [16] and Agent Security Bench [17] as representative and complementary evaluation environments; extending coverage to additional benchmarks and real-world deployment settings remains a natural next step. Future work should expand the threat model to broader multi-hop LLM infrastructures and more diverse agent deployments. On the mitigation side, an important next step is to design and evaluate principled integrity mechanisms, such as provider-signed responses or attested relay execution, that can restore end-to-end authenticity after relay-side TLS termination.

10 Related Work

Relay Infrastructure. LLM relays are widely deployed for API unification, cost optimization, model routing, and BYOK-style deployment [76, 77, 78, 79, 80]. Recent work increasingly treats these intermediaries as part of the LLM supply chain rather than as transparent transport infrastructure [32, 20]. This concern is reinforced by the TeamPCP compromise of LiteLLM [81] and by studies of privacy leakage and cross-tool harvesting in agentic and multi-agent systems [82, 83]. Closest to our work, Liu et al. [20] study Router-in-the-Middle attacks and measure malicious LLM routers in real deployments, showing that intermediary abuse already occurs in the wild. Our work asks a different question: once such an intermediary sits on the LLM–agent path, what security property is lost? We show that the relay position creates a response-path integrity failure between the model’s alignment-approved output and the agent’s execution input. This distinction separates relay tampering from prompt injection: the adversary need not persuade the model to emit unsafe content, but can instead substitute schema-valid execution fields after generation. Thus, prior and concurrent work establishes the existence and ecosystem impact of malicious intermediaries, while our work characterizes the structural post-alignment failure mode they enable and studies its exploitation and detection at the agent layer.

Prompt Injection and Agent Vulnerabilities. Prior work on prompt injection studies how user and argentic environment text can acquire unintended control authority in LLM agents, causing unexpected or policy-violating behavior. The core failure is the collapse of the data–instruction boundary inside the model–agent reasoning loop. Existing work covers direct injection through user-facing inputs [48, 84, 52, 53, 54, 85, 55, 56, 86] and indirect injection through retrieved documents, web pages, tool observations, or other external artifacts [51, 87, 83, 88, 89, 90]. Relay tampering targets a different boundary. It modifies the response delivered to the agent after model generation, making the failure one of post-alignment response integrity.

Guardrails and System-Level Defenses. Existing defenses mainly harden the model-agent reasoning loop against unintended instruction following. Content-channel defenses place classifiers, or filters at input or output interfaces, ranging from perplexity-based detectors [91] to the Llama Guard family, ShieldGemma, WildGuard, Granite Guardian, and NeMo Guardrails [92, 93, 94, 95, 96, 97]. These mechanisms inspect textual content and can degrade when instructions are contextually embedded or disguised [98, 99]. Runtime defenses instead constrain agent execution through privilege separation [100], sandboxing [101], consistency checks [102, 103], and shadow-model monitoring [104]. Model-side defenses train the backend LLM to better prioritize trusted instructions over untrusted inputs [105]. These defenses address instruction-boundary failures, where untrusted text influences the LLM before an action is selected. They do not provide end-to-end integrity for the response path in a relay-mediated setting. A malicious relay can leave the query unchanged, wait for the backend LLM to produce an aligned response, and then rewrite execution-bearing fields before the frontend agent receives them. Thus the input/output hardening and model alignment cannot guarantee that the action executed by the agent corresponds to the response generated by the backend LLM.

11 Conclusion

We identify post-alignment tampering, a structural integrity failure in BYOK relays that strictly dominates prompt injection, and instantiate it as RTA, achieving up to 99.1%99.1\% ASR across six LLMs while keeping 74%74\% of its latency overhead within natural network variance. Existing agent-side defenses fail to close this gap; our time-channel detector reaches 0.9640.964 AUC at n=50n{=}50 turns, motivating end-to-end response integrity as a first-class primitive in future LLM API protocols.
